planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun with room to reach its mature 6-7 foot height; tolerates a range of soils but performs best with consistent moisture during establishment.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun with room to reach its mature 6-7 foot height. Bred by German nurseryman Ernst Pagels to flower reliably even in cooler, shorter-season climates, Malepartus produces broad green foliage with a fine white midrib and sends up large, silky plumes in late summer well ahead of most other Miscanthus sinensis selections. The plumes open a warm pinkish-copper, deepen to rust-red through fall, and finally fade to shimmering silvery-white, persisting well into winter above a strong, upright-arching clump. Foliage turns shades of orange, red, and bronze in autumn, adding a second season of color before the plant is cut back hard in late winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cut back to a few inches before new growth emerges in spring.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. One of the oldest and most influential Miscanthus sinensis cultivars in the trade, Silberfeder forms a large upright-arching clump of narrow green leaves topped in late summer by tall, airy plumes that open sparkling pinkish-silver and mature to shining silvery-white by fall. It is among the tallest garden-scale maiden grasses, often reaching 7 to 8 feet in flower, making it best suited to large borders, screens, or specimen use rather than small beds. The foliage turns a soft wheat tone in autumn and the seed heads remain attractive and structurally sound through much of winter.

common_name: Gold Bar Miscanthus (Dwarf Banded Zebra Grass)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; divide clumps every few years to maintain vigor and banding intensity.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing clumps every few years to maintain vigor and banding intensity. Discovered as an open-pollinated seedling of the banded cultivar Strictus, Gold Bar carries the same horizontal creamy-yellow banding but on a shorter, denser, more rigidly upright plant with far more numerous bands per leaf blade, giving it a bolder striped look than its parent. Flowering later in the season than most maiden grasses, it produces coppery-bronze plumes above the compact clump in late fall in warmer zones. Its small stature relative to typical Miscanthus sinensis makes it useful as an accent or specimen in gardens too small for full-size zebra or porcupine grass.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in reasonably drained soil; drought-tolerant once established and fits easily into small residential gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun in reasonably drained soil; this drought-tolerant selection asks for little beyond a sunny spot once established. Named for Japan's Yaku Island, this selection is the most diminutive commonly grown form of Miscanthus sinensis, forming a tidy, fine-textured clump of narrow, gracefully arching green blades well under half the size of the species. Buff-colored plumes with a light reddish tinge appear in late summer, rising just above the foliage before fading to silver and persisting into winter. Its compact size makes it far more versatile than full-size maiden grasses, fitting easily into mixed perennial borders, foundation plantings, and smaller residential gardens.

planting.note: Plant in full sun with even moisture; tolerates damp clay soils and light shade but struggles where summers are consistently hot and humid.

directions: Plant in full sun with even moisture, though it tolerates damp clay soils and light shade. Avalanche carries a crisp white central stripe down each narrow green leaf blade, the reverse variegation pattern of the more common Overdam, and holds its color and upright habit through summer heat better than many variegated grasses. It forms a neat, sterile clump that sends up slender flower stems in early summer, opening pinkish-green and maturing to a warm wheat color that stands through winter. Because it does not set viable seed, Avalanche stays contained rather than self-sowing, making it a tidy, well-mannered choice for formal borders and mass plantings.
